citations.desc: Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC).
citations.narrative:
IACUC approved protocol #A26-001 lacked an adequate description for the provision of appropriate sedatives,
analgesics, or anesthetics for procedures that may cause more than momentary or slight pain or distress to the animals.
The protocol stated, “On day 7…anesthesia and analgesia will proceed following table 3’s dosing strategy.” The table
listed four medications and a mg/kg dose. However, no route or frequency was provided and no indication of which
medications would be used for analgesia versus anesthesia. In addition, the protocol stated, “…technician will administer
analgesia with oral??? each day following surgery…” No further information regarding which medication, route, or
frequency was provided as required in section (iv)(a).
The protocol also lacked a method of assessment to determine the point at which an animal that would otherwise
experience severe or chronic pain or distress that cannot be relieved will be painlessly euthanized at the end of the
procedure, or if appropriate, during the procedure as required in section (v).
Per this Section, the IACUC must conduct a review of those components of the activities related to the care and use of
animals and determine that the proposed activities are in accordance with this subchapter of the AWA. The IACUC shall
address the items identified in this protocol.
Correct by July 15, 2026.

citations.desc: Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC).
citations.narrative:
IACUC approved protocol #A26-001 did not contain a complete written description of the proposed use of animals.
The protocol lacked a complete description of a procedure to place a sponge in the left middle meatus, nasal cavity, under
endoscopic guidance. The registrant indicated the procedure was performed under anesthesia, however there was no
description of a sedated or anesthetic procedure, preparation for the procedure, or analgesia.
Per this Section, proposals to conduct an activity involving animals must contain a complete description of the proposed
use of the animals so the IACUC can determine during its review that all components of the animal use proposal are in
accordance with the requirements as outlined in this subchapter of the AWA. The IACUC needs to address this item
identified for this protocol.
Correct by July 15, 2026

The facility has not maintained all required records of IACUC activities.
There was no record of minutes documented for the IACUC meeting held in April 2026 available for review at the time of
inspection as required by (a)(1) of this section.
The facility was unable to provide documentation of IACUC approval of an active Animal Use Protocol, A26-001, currently
in use for regulated species as required by (a)(2) of this section.
According to the registrant, the IACUC conducted the semi-annual program review and inspection in April 2026. However,
there is no documentation that the IACUC prepared, reviewed, and submitted a report of the Committee's evaluations to
the Institutional Official, as required by paragraph (a)(3) of this section.
Maintaining meeting minutes, documentation of protocol approval, and documentation of semi-annual inspections is
important to document IACUC activities and helps demonstrate the functionality of the IACUC. Each research facility must
maintain IACUC records including meeting minutes, records of attendance, activities of the Committee, and Committee
deliberations. The facility must also maintain records of proposed activities involving animals and whether IACUC
approval was given or withheld; and records of semiannual IACUC reports prepared and forwarded to the Institutional
Official.
Correct by July 25, 2026

The indoor enclosures of three rabbits were not structurally sound, were in disrepair, and not suitable for the species. The
enclosures were made for chickens and have approximately 2-inch gaps running the full length of the front of the cage
near the bottom to facilitate retrieval of eggs. Due to the weight of the rabbits, the bottoms of the cages are sagging
resulting in the gaps becoming larger near the center of the front of the enclosure and bending of the wire mesh creating a
sharp point where the mesh broke which may cause injury. The gaps in the wire mesh also pose a risk of injury to the
rabbits due to entrapment of the digits/feet/legs/etc.
Per this Section, primary enclosures shall be structurally sound and maintained in good repair to protect the rabbits from
injury. The Registrant must address the gaps and structural integrity of the enclosures to ensure the health and safety of
the rabbits.
Correct by July 15,2026.
This inspection and exit interview were conducted with a facility representative.
